title: Architecture & Standards: API, Coding, Infra, Model-Serving, Observability, Performance, and ADR Process
author: Priya Kapoor
body:
Summary

This document consolidates Redwood Inference’s architecture and engineering standards across API, coding, infrastructure, model-serving, observability, performance, and the ADR (Architecture Decision Record) process. It is intended to be a canonical, high-level reference for engineering teams making design choices that affect latency, cost, reliability, and security for inference services.

Goals
- Provide clear, actionable standards that minimize cross-team integration friction.
- Ensure predictable production characteristics (latency, throughput, cost).
- Make trade-offs explicit via ADRs and link decisions to measurable SLOs and ownership.

Scope
Applies to all backend services that are part of the inference platform, customer-facing APIs, infra provisioning for Dedicated/Private products, and model-serving runtime components. Does not cover client SDK UI/UX details or marketing assets.

1) API Standards

Intro
Redwood exposes both internal and public REST/JSON endpoints and gRPC where low latency/binary payloads are required. The API design must prioritize stable contracts, backward compatibility, observability hooks, and schema validation.

Rules
- Public API surface must be versioned (/v1, /v2) and semantic changes require a new major version.
- Prefer JSON-over-HTTP for customer-facing endpoints, gRPC for high-throughput internal service-to-service calls.
- All request/response payloads must include a version metadata field for compatibility testing: {"api_version": "v1"}.
- Use OpenAPI v3 for all REST endpoints; include examples for common operations.
- Responses must follow the standard envelope: {"data": ..., "meta": {"request_id": ..., "processing_ms": ...}, "errors": [...]}.
- Explicit error codes and types; map to HTTP status codes and include a machine-readable error_code (e.g., INFERENCE_MODEL_NOT_FOUND).
- Timeouts: default client-visible timeout is 30s for generation endpoints; internal service-to-service timeouts should be 3x the expected p95 latency.
- Idempotency: long-running requests (batch jobs, model-ops) must provide idempotency keys and return an operation resource.
- Authentication: all endpoints require an API key with RBAC; headers: Authorization: Bearer <token> and X-Request-ID optional but recommended.

Example OpenAPI snippet (required in service repo):

  paths:
    /v1/generate:
      post:
        summary: Generate text
        requestBody:
          content:
            application/json:
              schema:
                $ref: '#/components/schemas/GenerationRequest'

2) Coding Standards

Principles
- Readability and small surface area for critical inference paths.
- Safety checks and input validation close to the edges.
- Automated linting and type checking enforced in CI.

Requirements
- Language-specific style guides: Go for infra/control-plane services, Rust/C++ for latency-critical runtime components, Python for orchestration/eval scripts.
- Unit tests: min 80% coverage for core packages; critical runtime kernels require >=90% and regression tests.
- Linters: golangci-lint for Go, rustfmt + clippy for Rust, black + ruff for Python. CI must fail on new lint errors.
- Dependency policy: no direct runtime dependencies with low-maintenance or risky licenses without Security approval. Use the dependency approval checklist.
- Feature flags: all behavioral changes must be behind a feature flag for canary/rollback.

Code organization recommendations
- Keep inference-critical loops in a single package/module to limit cross-module allocations and GC pressure.
- Explicit boundaries between control plane, data plane, and model runtime.

3) Infrastructure Standards

Provisioning & IaC
- All cloud infra must be defined in Terraform modules under terraform-and-iac with environment overlays. No ad-hoc console changes.
- Use a shared module for GPU pools with standard tagging, autoscaling policies, and quotas.
- Secrets must be stored in KMS-backed vault; never check credentials into git.

Networking & Security
- VPCs limited by product (hosted vs dedicated vs private). Private deployments must support customer-managed VPC peering and AWS PrivateLink equivalents.
- RBAC at least RBAC + least privilege for service accounts. Network policies should restrict pod-to-pod traffic for sensitive services (model KV cache, auth).
- TLS everywhere: mTLS for internal RPC by default.

Capacity & Cost Controls
- GPU autoscaling policy defaults: target 70% utilization for steady-state, scale up at 80% and scale down below 50% with a 10-minute cooldown.
- Cost alerts: monthly projected spend > 90% of committed budget triggers PagerDuty to Finance + Eng Infra.

4) Model-Serving Standards

Runtime behavior
- Runtime must expose a stable model manifest for each model version: model_id, commit_hash, flavor (fp32/int8), kv_cache_behavior, max_sequence_length.
- Model onboarding checklist (required in model-onboarding): unit/regression tests, perf profile, quantization profile, safety review, and ADR if architecture changes are required.
- Default inference mode: streaming tokens where possible; fallbacks to synchronous chunked responses for legacy clients.

KV cache, batching, and quantization
- KV cache semantics must be documented and have explicit TTLs; cache invalidation events should be emitted to observability.
- Batching configuration: define max_batch_size and max_wait_ms per route. Defaults: max_batch_size=64, max_wait_ms=8ms for Hosted; Dedicated may tune to higher batch sizes.
- Quantization profiles: each model variant must include an approved quantization profile (e.g., int8-fp16 mix) and quality budget (max tolerated BLEU/ROUGE/semantic drift).

Compatibility & Rollout
- Backward compatibility: new kernels or quantization must be canaried against a production prompt set (see Evals in applied-ml-and-evals).
- Rollout steps: canary -> ramp (10%, 25%, 50%, 100%) with automated quality checks at each stage.

5) Observability Standards

Telemetry requirements
- Traces: all RPCs must propagate and log a trace context (W3C traceparent).
- Metrics: standard metric family for inference endpoints: request_count, request_latency_ms{p50,p90,p95,p99}, token_count, model_cache_hit_rate, batch_size.
- Logs: structured JSON logs with fields: timestamp, level, service, env, request_id, model_id, user_id (obfuscated), error_code, latency_ms.
- SLO/event correlation: spans and logs must include an eval_run_id when traffic is part of an evaluation.

Dashboards & Alerts
- Per-service dashboard: p95 latency, error rate (5xx), saturation (CPU/GPU/memory), queue depth, and cost per token estimate.
- Alert thresholds (default): p95 latency > target_latency * 2 for 5 minutes -> page-on-call. Error rate > 1% for 5 minutes -> page. GPU memory OOM errors -> immediate page.

6) Performance Standards and SLOs

SLO structure
- Each public inference route must publish: target p50/p95 latency, throughput (tokens/sec), availability (% uptime), and cost per 1k tokens.
- Example SLO for hosted low-latency text generation (v1): availability 99.9% monthly, p95 latency <= 350ms for <=256 token requests, error budget 43.2 minutes/month.

Benchmarking
- Master benchmarking harness maintained in eng-serving-runtime/benchmarking-and-perf-suite. All changes to serving runtime kernels must include end-to-end benchmarks (latency, throughput, tail latency) and regression thresholds.
- Perf regression process: if a PR causes >3% increase in p95 latency for a canonical workload, it must be reverted or include a mitigation plan documented in the PR.

Performance testing checklist
1. Reproduce baseline on the perf suite.
2. Run regression tests with synthetic and recorded production traces.
3. Validate memory/GPU utilization and peak allocation.
4. Attach benchmark artifacts to the PR and link the results in the ADR if the change is architectural.

7) ADR (Architecture Decision Record) Process

Purpose
Use ADRs to record important architecture decisions that have cross-team impact, encapsulate trade-offs, and provide linkable history for future engineers. ADRs are required for changes that affect API contracts, infra topology, model runtime semantics, SLOs, or security posture.

When to write an ADR
- Introducing a new public API or changing an API contract.
- Significant infra topology changes (e.g., introducing a new region, replacing a GPU scheduler).
- Runtime kernel or model-serving semantic changes (e.g., KV cache semantics).
- Changes that materially impact cost model or SLOs.

ADR template (must be a top-level repo file and in confluence):
| Field | Value |
|-------|-------|
| Title | Short descriptive name |
| Status | proposed | approved | deprecated | superseded |
| Date | YYYY-MM-DD |
| Authors | list of authors |
| Context | Background and why this matters |
| Decision | What we decided to do |
| Consequences | Operational and technical consequences |
| Rollout plan | Canary + ramp steps and SLO validation |
| Revert plan | Steps to revert if metrics fail |

ADR process steps (numbered)
1. Draft: author creates ADR in ADR repo and a confluence stub linking to the ADR.
2. Review: assign at least two reviewers from impacted teams (infra, runtime, product).
3. Approval: owner_team or platform architecture lead approves.
4. Publish: set ADR status to approved and link to implementation tasks in planning board.
5. Postmortem: after rollout, update ADR with lessons learned and change status if superseded.

Example ADR summary (short):
- Title: Standardize KV cache TTL semantics for hosted inference
- Status: approved (2026-06-15)
- Decision: Add explicit per-model TTLs and include eviction events in telemetry.
- Consequences: Small storage overhead; enables easier cache debugging and deterministic fallback behaviors.

Governance and Ownership
- Each ADR must identify an owner (oncall/team). The architecture guild maintains a ledger of ADRs and tracks open decisions.
- Periodic review: ADRs older than 18 months should be reviewed for relevance.

8) Operational Playbooks & Runbooks (linking)
- All standards above must have an associated runbook for oncall responders; see eng-developer-experience/runbooks and eng-sre/runbooks.
- Runbooks must include: quick mitigation steps, escalation path, rollback commands, and dashboard links.

9) Compliance & Auditability
- Audit logs for model-serving and admin actions retained per data-residency-and-retention policy.
- Changes to infra and model manifests must be auditable with commit hashes and change descriptions.

10) Appendices
A. Default threshold table
| Metric | Default threshold | Paging behavior | Owner |
|--------|-------------------|-----------------|-------|
| p95 latency (gen) | 2x target for 5m | Page | eng-serving-runtime |
| Error rate (5xx) | >1% (5m) | Page | eng-sre |
| GPU OOM | any occurrence | Immediate page | eng-infra |

B. Example structured log JSON
{
  "timestamp": "2026-12-18T15:04:05Z",
  "level": "info",
  "service": "inference-router",
  "env": "prod",
  "request_id": "req_12345",
  "model_id": "rwd-llama3-13b-int8",
  "user_id": "u_6789",
  "latency_ms": 312,
  "tokens": 128
}

C. Quick ADR checklist (for PRs that require an ADR)
- [ ] Draft ADR in ADR repo with template populated
- [ ] Add confluence stub linking to ADR and affected docs
- [ ] Add reviewers from platform/infrastructure/product
- [ ] Run perf and quality regressions and attach results
- [ ] Include rollout and revert plans

Related resources
- Model onboarding checklist: /confluence/applied-ml-and-evals/model-onboarding
- Perf suite: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/benchmarking-and-perf-suite
- ADR repo (git): github.com/redwood-inference/architecture/adr

Contact & governance
Questions about these standards should be raised in the #architecture-guild Slack channel or sent to architecture@redwood.dev. The architecture guild and the platform team jointly maintain this doc and the ADR ledger.
